idiom_name: abstract class CustomerDao with pure virtual methods + per-store adapter (std::unique_ptr ownership)
implementation_notes: C++ supplies the interface machinery - a class with pure virtual functions is an abstract class that cannot be instantiated - but no standard-library persistence layer, so the DAO structure is hand-written: one abstract base per aggregate in domain terms, one adapter per store owning the connection, and unique_ptr/reference ownership so the client never touches the driver. What replaces the classic form when only one store will ever exist is a concrete class (or a template/CRTP helper) with no virtual dispatch; the abstract base earns its cost only when the store must be swapped or mocked.
pitfalls: A non-virtual destructor on the base class (or taking the DAO by value) makes cleanup undefined behaviour; make the destructor virtual and hold DAOs by reference or unique_ptr.
Virtual dispatch plus one adapter per store costs an extra indirection and a second class hierarchy once a factory is added - do not pay it when a single store exists.
Returning sqlite3_step's result code or letting a driver exception escape hands the client the store's vocabulary; define your own error type at the interface boundary.

variants.name: Boost.MySQL coroutine DAO over an Asio io_context
variants.idiom_name: co_await conn.async_execute(...) with Boost.MySQL and Asio
variants.implementation_notes: The same DAO contract can be asynchronous: Boost.MySQL runs statements through an Asio io_context with async_execute, and C++20 stackless coroutines let the adapter await them instead of nesting completion handlers, so the interface either returns awaitable types or accepts a completion token. Choose it when the application is already Asio-based and a thread blocking on a classic JDBC-style call would stall the executor; keep the synchronous abstract-base form when call sites are thread-based and the extra coroutine machinery buys nothing. Trade-off versus the callback variant is the same as everywhere: linear code and simpler error propagation, at the cost of frame lifetime rules I must obey.
pitfalls: The coroutine frame owns the statement text, bound parameters and results: returning a reference to anything stored in the frame (or to the DAO) is a dangling-coroutine bug.
Mixing a blocking driver call into a coroutine stalls the whole io_context; every store call in the async variant must be awaited.
